I looked outside and could see men running around. I noticed that a lot of them were wearing red and green headbands. They were dressed mostly in camouflage uniforms, although some also wore a mixture of civilian and military clothing."

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So on this occasion you didn't notice insignia of any kind on them; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the paragraph starting with "I decided to go to Reuf's house," the last sentence you will see it, when you're talking about the people in your yard, you said, "I was not able to see any insignia but most of them had either red or green bands tied somewhere, either as a headband, an armband, or hanging from an epaulette." So again, even though you were asked about this, you couldn't confirm that those persons were wearing any kind of bands; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw this when I looked into my yard.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: However, in your statement it says that you didn't see it. So these two statements differ, don't they?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand you. I didn't see any insignia, but most of them had these bands. When I said "patches," I meant insignia. I didn't see that, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were asked again, and on page 6, 03004129 - that's the ERN number - you said: "The next morning, on the 24th of July, three BH army soldiers came to Tomas's house. All three were wearing green camouflage uniforms and were wearing coloured bands." So again you didn't notice the insignia you testified about here in court.

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO [Resumed]
utterances.text: At least, that is what I said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On page 10, or ERN number 03004133, in a paragraph saying "Back in our cell," et cetera, et cetera, the one-but-last sentence says: "The guards always wore green camouflage uniforms. I think they were soldiers, but I didn't notice whether they wore the insignia of units or not." So, Mr. Mrso, is it true that you were asked five times to describe the soldiers on various occasions and that never once did you mention that they wore the insignia of the MOS? Is that what it says in this statement?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is what it says.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While you were still in the elementary school, in the gym of the elementary school called Aleksic [as interpreted], family members were allowed to bring food to the detainees because the food you were given was quite insufficient; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether it was allowed, but we heard outside noise. People were demanding to hand in something. Now, whether somebody let them do that or not, I don't know that, madam.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When on the 5th of August you were released, you went home and you saw that it was being looked after by your neighbour Reuf, thanks to whom the house was no longer touched nor had anyone moved into it; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After your release, you opened an HDZ office in the parish house, and together with the parson you took care of the Croats who stayed behind in Bugojno; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you could put it that way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Because of the war and the fact that many people of Bugojno were leaving Bugojno, prior to the outbreak of the conflict only 7.000 Croats had stayed in Bugojno; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During combat operations, together with a part of the HVO Brigade and the Home Guard Battalion, Bugojno was left by about 3.000 inhabitants.

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not what I stated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After your release, there were about 2.600 to 3.000 citizens of Bugojno of Croat ethnicity left.

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is what I said, and that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Up until the end of the war only 900 Croats remained in Bugojno.

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said by the end of 1993 we listed the people and there were about 900 Croats in the municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Throughout that period of time, until the exchange, you visited prisoners of war at the Iskra Stadium.

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't visit them. They allowed me once across the wire fence to speak to some people who were in the camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At that time, in addition to the shortage of food in Bugojno, there was no water in Bugojno; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Actually, sources of water through which the town was supplied were in the hands of the HVO, which for military reasons frequently would not allow water to reach the town; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is. I beg your pardon. At the time I didn't know who was behind the fact that there was no water.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thanks to your efforts and due to this fact too, the prisoners Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. were allowed to go home under escort and to take care of their hygiene, to wash, to have a bath, et cetera; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is right. Not just to go home. Many of them no longer had family members left. But they went to see their friends, acquaintances, and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Also, throughout that period of time detainees were allowed through Caritas and also through family members and acquaintances to be given food.

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Regarding the situation which you followed in Bugojno, while in Grude you informed the president of the HDZ and the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, Mr. Mate Boban, about that situation, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mrso. I have no further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I turn now to the other Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. As Mr. Kubura is not charged with any of the incidents that the witness has testified about, we have no questions on behalf of Mr. Kubura. I'm grateful, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Dixon. I turn again to the Prosecution to see whether they have any additional questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. The Prosecution has no questions in re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I'm going to return to the Defence these documents, as you are not asking them to be admitted into evidence. So I'm going to return to you these documents. Just a small point of clarification regarding the documents regarding the Prosecution: The witness told us a moment ago that he wanted a copy of his written statement. And I looked at the English version, and indeed on the 15th of September, 2000, the witness did put a note in handwriting. And we understand that he wanted a copy of this statement. Then what he said in his language should have been translated, and I don't see any translation of that request. However, as the document is not being tendered, there's no problem. But if this document were to be exhibited, then this would be a difficulty. So I am returning these documents now to the Defence. Madam Usher is going to collect the documents. Mr. Mrso, you testified for two days. We wish to thank you for coming to The Hague. You answered questions from the Prosecution, questions from the Defence, as well as questions put to you by the Judges. We thank you for your testimony, and we wish you a safe journey home. And I would like to ask Madam Usher to accompany you out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour, Mr. President. I wish to thank you too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us continue the hearing. We have another witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, sir. You have been called as a witness by the Prosecution. I just wish to check whether you can hear the translation of my words in your own language properly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can hear you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. As you are about to testify, you first have to tell me your first and last name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My name is Zrinko Alvir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And when were you born?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 25th of October, 1958.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And where were you born?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Bugojno.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is your current occupation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm a driver.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And in 1993, more than ten years ago, what was your occupation then? What were you doing, if you can still remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] During the war or before the war?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1993.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1993, I was a military policeman.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. As you have been called as a witness, I need to ask you to read the solemn declaration that will be given to you by Madam Usher. Please read the text in your own language.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before giving the floor to the Prosecution, I wish to give you some information regarding the proceedings here. You will first answer questions that will be put to you by a representative of the Prosecution; and she's on your right. After those questions, the attorneys of the accused, who are seated on your left - there are six of them - will also have questions for you. Not all six of them; only two of them. And they will ask you questions in your own language. The three Judges, in front of you, may also if they consider it useful, to ask you any questions they may wish for clarification purposes. The questions that will be put to you by the Prosecution or by the Defence require answers from you that should be complete and precise because through your answers you will be informing the Chamber about the events of which you were an eyewitness. If you don't understand the meaning of a question, ask the person putting it to you to rephrase it. If there's any difficulty, tell us what it is. We are here to resolve that type of difficulty. As you know, you have pledged to tell the whole truth, which means that you mustn't testify falsely, because if you lie in the course of your examination, you are risking prosecution for false testimony, and such prosecution can result in fines or imprisonment or even both. However, as you have solemnly sworn to tell the whole truth, we expect you to answer perfectly the questions that will be put to you. Also, it is my duty to tell you that the words you are going to speak cannot be used against you. If you do not wish to answer a question, explain why not and the Chamber will judge whether it is necessary to ask you to answer nevertheless. Have you already testified in a court of law before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So this is the first time. I see. So I felt it necessary to explain all this for you so as to assist you. I'm now going to turn to Ms. Benjamin. I think she is the one who's going to carry out the examination-in-chief. And I give you the floor, madam.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Examined by Ms. Henry-Benjamin:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Alvir. You indicated to the Trial Chamber that you were born in Bugojno. Could you tell the Chamber in which municipality Bugojno is located.

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO ALVIR
utterances.text: Bugojno is a municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you give us an idea of the ethnic breakdown of Bugojno, please.

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO ALVIR
utterances.text: Bugojno was inhabited by Croats, Muslims, and Serbs. I think about -- there were more or less an equal number of Muslims and Croats. Serbs were slightly less numerous, about ten or so thousand of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Alvir, did you ever do service with the JNA, compulsory national service with the JNA?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO ALVIR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you tell the Trial Chamber for how long.

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO ALVIR
utterances.text: It was 15 months, but there was a shortening by one month, so a total of 14 months is the period I served.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you state for us what was your assignment while you were in the JNA.

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO ALVIR
utterances.text: I was a driver as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever enlist in any other military body?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO ALVIR
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you ever a member of any other army?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO ALVIR
utterances.text: During the war, of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where were you based?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO ALVIR
utterances.text: In Bugojno, in the Kalin Hotel.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you assist the Trial Chamber with who was in command of your battalion in the HVO -- your unit.

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO ALVIR
utterances.text: Mr. Stipica Zelic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you live prior to the conflict?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO ALVIR
utterances.text: In Bugojno.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Or where did you live at the time of the conflict, during the conflict?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO ALVIR
utterances.text: Also in Bugojno.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you assist the Trial Chamber: In the middle of July 1993, what took place in Bugojno?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO ALVIR
utterances.text: A conflict broke out between Croats and Muslims in Bugojno. And when Bugojno fell -- I don't know how to explain it -- we, the members of the HVO, were imprisoned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When the conflict broke out, are you aware of any arrangement or agreement with -- that was made between your commander and anyone else?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO ALVIR
utterances.text: During the conflict, when everything was already in the hands of the Muslim army, our commander went to talk to their commander at the grammar school because they were accommodated in the grammar school building. He went to negotiate our surrender, members of the HVO from the Kalin Hotel. And then, when Mr. Stipica returned, a surrender had been arranged and then we left the Kalin Hotel without our weapons in front of the city cafe in Bugojno, the central cafe in Bugojno.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the time when you left the hotel, were there civilians in the hotel?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO ALVIR
utterances.text: Yes, there were about 150 civilians from Gaj who had withdrawn when Gaj fell. And they went to the Hotel Kalin, where we were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you said to the Trial Chamber that upon the return of your commander you gave up your guns and you were sent to the parking lot. Could you tell us how many -- how many of yourselves, of your group of soldiers, were lined up in the parking lot.

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO ALVIR
utterances.text: There were about 100 soldiers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, Mr. Alvir, could you kindly describe for us what took place, what was the procedure that followed once you got to the parking lot.

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO ALVIR
utterances.text: When we got to the parking lot, we were lined up two by two. And then they searched us to see what papers we had on us. They looked through our pockets. We had to hand over our papers and take everything out of our pockets. All the badges that we had had to be turned over. And then they took us to the furniture shop two by two, and that is where they detained us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, for the benefit of the Trial Chamber, could you describe for us what you mean or who you mean when you say "they."

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO ALVIR
utterances.text: Well, the Muslim army, the BH army, whatever you want to call it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you be able to describe how they were dressed?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO ALVIR
utterances.text: They were wearing military camouflage uniforms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And would you be able to assist us with where the furniture room was located?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO ALVIR
utterances.text: The furniture shop was in the centre of the town. It was about a kilometre, a kilometre and a half from the Kalin Hotel, and from the police station in Bugojno it was about 100 to 150 metres further away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you describe the physical appearance of the room, the furniture room. Could you describe the physical appearance to the Court, please.

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO ALVIR
utterances.text: Well, it was a fairly big room in the furniture shop. The outside walls were made of glass. It also had a basement area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in what part of this room were you?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO ALVIR
utterances.text: We were kept in the basement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sorry. Could you describe for us, then, the conditions in the basement of the furniture room.

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO ALVIR
utterances.text: The rooms were dark. There was no light in them. There was about 10 centimetres of water in that room. There were wooden planks of some kind and we would sit on them and sleep on them. And between the planks there was water; it was about 10 centimetres deep.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Approximately how many of you were in this room?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO ALVIR
utterances.text: Well, there were about 100 people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you give us an approximate measurement of the dimensions of the room.

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO ALVIR
utterances.text: I don't know exactly, but the room was perhaps 5 or 6 metres by 6 or 7 metres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, what about the conditions in the room? How were your bathroom facilities?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO ALVIR
utterances.text: There weren't any bathroom facilities in the basement. There were some on the ground floor; there was a toilet up there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you eat? How did you get food? Did you eat? How did you eat?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO ALVIR
utterances.text: For the first few days Sister Pavka and Ranko brought us food. Afterwards, we received food once a day from the members of the army, too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your initial days at the furniture room or the basement of the furniture room, that is, explain to us how you actually relieved yourselves. Because you said the toilet was on the upper floor. How did you relieve yourselves on the first few days in the basement?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO ALVIR
utterances.text: During the first few days, we couldn't go out. They wouldn't allow us. So on the whole, people relieved themselves in the basement. It was only later that they allowed people to go up to the toilet.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Alvir, let us first take the very first day of your detention at the furniture room. Could you tell the Trial Chamber what transpired.

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO ALVIR
utterances.text: The first day we were taken to the furniture shop, they searched us again. They searched through our pockets and everything else to see whether we had anything on us. And then they ordered us to go down into the basement. After that, they took us out one by one. They took away our military equipment, our clothes, shirts, trousers, jackets, and they would give us their torn clothes in exchange. Then in the evening, there was a roll-call and they started beating people. They started beating some of my colleagues. I was the last one in that group.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I know that the -- the basement was dark, so could you tell us where or could you tell us where your colleagues and yourself were taken to when the roll-call was called. Were you taken away from the basement?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO ALVIR
utterances.text: We were taken up to the ground floor. We went out of the basement, went up to the ground floor. So that was the area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were you able to recognise any of these names that were called?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO ALVIR
utterances.text: Of my colleagues?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO ALVIR
utterances.text: Ivica Kajic, Ante Sekelja, Ante Palinic, Stipica Zelic. I was the last one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And for the Trial Chamber, could you tell -- could you state what was the ethnic background of these -- your colleagues that were called.

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO ALVIR
utterances.text: They were all Croats.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you were the last to be called, so you were in the basement when everybody else was called. Could you tell us if you heard anything from your point at the bottom of the basement.

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO ALVIR
utterances.text: Well, you could hear the sound of beating. You could hear the people groaning. The people who were being beaten were groaning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When your name was called, did you go to the ground floor?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO ALVIR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Describe for the Trial Chamber what transpired when your name was called and you reported to the ground floor of the furniture room.

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO ALVIR
utterances.text: I went up to the ground floor, and as soon as I got up there they told me to lie down and to spread out my arms and legs. I was told to lie down on my stomach and to spread out my arms and legs. Then they started beating me with batons. They started kicking me and trampling me. And they would tread on my -- on my fingers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During this time, were you interrogated in any way?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO ALVIR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And could you assist us with the topic of the interrogation.

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO ALVIR
utterances.text: On the whole, it had to do with the positions of the HVO. They wanted to know the location of certain people, the responsibility of certain people. Those were the subjects I was asked about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you repeat over and over that they wanted to know about the HVO, they tramped on my fingers. Could you tell this Trial Chamber who you refer to when you say "they."

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO ALVIR
utterances.text: Well, I'm referring to those soldiers who questioned us and who beat us. That's who I'm referring to. These are the soldiers from the BH army or from the Muslim army, as they called them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, this beating that you told us started from the first night that you were there and the procedure of calling roll-call and going upstairs, was this a nightly affair? Did this occur every night?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO ALVIR
utterances.text: On the whole, it happened at night, and it happened every night.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you indicate to the Trial Chamber what was the significance of the night of August 5th, 1993, as it relates to you personally.

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO ALVIR
utterances.text: On that night, we already thought that no one was going to be called out. It was one of the calmest nights, until 3.00 or 4.00 in the morning. Then they called me out first. I went up. I was immediately hit as soon as I appeared on the ground floor. I think I was hit with some sort of a wooden stick. I fell on the floor because of the blow. And then they continued beating me with some sort of iron tubes. They were nickel metal iron tubes. And this would make your skin break as soon as they hit you with these things. This went on for about half an hour or 40 minutes, at least.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At this session, were you interrogated in any way?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO ALVIR
utterances.text: Yes. On the whole, they asked about various people, wanted to know what sort of positions they held, what sort of duties they performed in the HVO, where they had been, and so forth.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you threatened in any way?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO ALVIR
utterances.text: Well, of course I was threatened. They'd point their rifles at your forehead, and they would say, "We'll kill you now." All sorts of things happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In particular, the 5th of August, 1993, in the wee hours of the morning, 3.00, were you able to recognise your beaters?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO ALVIR
utterances.text: Yes. I recognised two of them immediately, that very night.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And would you happen to have known their names or know them personally?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO ALVIR
utterances.text: Yes. I knew them very well. They were men from the town whom I knew and I would see them every day. One was Edin Vrban and Durakovic Sacir. There were some other men, Karadza. I didn't recognise the others. It was only subsequently that I found out their names.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And these two soldiers that you recognised, would you be able to assist us with what unit they may have come from?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO ALVIR
utterances.text: I don't know exactly the unit they came from. I know it was the BH army, as they called it, but as for the exact unit, I don't know. They had various numbers, the 107th and so on. So I wouldn't know which number their unit was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you completed your rounds of beating, and did you return to the basement?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO ALVIR
utterances.text: Yes. They ordered me to return to the basement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you returned to the basement, did you hear if other names were called?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO ALVIR
utterances.text: Before I returned, Dragan Brecic was called out, and then Mladen Havranek after him. This young man died because of the beating he had been given. And afterwards there was Frano Kosak and then Miroslav Marjanovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Mladen Havranek, he -- did he obey the command to go up to the ground floor? Did he obey?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO ALVIR
utterances.text: Yes. He had to obey.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And could you tell the Trial Chamber why he was up at the ground floor what you heard.

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO ALVIR
utterances.text: Well, the beating -- it was terrible to listen to the young man being beaten. When they told him to go down into the basement again, he wasn't able to do this on his own. They had to -- he asked Boro Divkovic to help him get back into the basement. He was a friend who slept next us. He called out to Boro Divkovic to help him go down. And Boro Divkovic and Branko Dadic helped him to return to the basement. After he returned, I asked him, "Mladen, did you recognise them?" He said no. I told him about the two men, that I had recognised them, he said he hadn't recognised them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And later that day, were you able to speak to Mladen Havranek again?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO ALVIR
utterances.text: No. That was the last time we spoke to each other. Afterwards he was sick, and the colleagues called out to the guards to take him outside because he was feeling sick. And 15 or 20 minutes later he probably died, because the colleagues who had taken him out said that he had died as a result of the beating he had been given.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you seen Mladen Havranek since that day?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO ALVIR
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Whilst in the basement of the furniture room, did you receive any treatment for your injuries?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO ALVIR
utterances.text: When Mladen died, they came for us. In fact, I think an ambulance came from the hospital, and we were transferred to the hospital then. They transferred me, Frano Kosak, Miroslav Marjanovic, and Dragan Brecic. They placed us in the hospital because they were afraid that our fate might be the same as that of Mladen Havranek. When we arrived in the hospital, they immediately gave us -- put us on a drip. And after I'd received this drip, I sat on the floor and I fell off the floor. I lost consciousness. I don't know how long I was out. A doctor came and splashed some water -- poured some water over me, and that's how I came to again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Excuse me. Mr. Alvir, could you define for the Court the injuries that you received on the 5th of August and prior to that in the basement of the furniture room.

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO ALVIR
utterances.text: Well, the injuries I had were from my knees up to my shoulders. And it was on the posterior part of the body. I was black and blue. I had a fracture of the fifth and sixth rib, too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There came a time when you were discharged from the hospital or you were released from the hospital. Could you tell us where you went to after your release.

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO ALVIR
utterances.text: When we were discharged from the hospital, they took us to the Iskra Stadium, the football stadium of the Iskra Football Club.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And could you describe for us the conditions at the stadium, please.

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO ALVIR
utterances.text: Well, on the whole, the rooms hadn't been completely constructed. There were some wooden planks on the floor, some blankets, and we would lie on these blankets and on these wooden planks. It was very crowded and we were packed in, like sardines in a can.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Approximately how many people would you say were housed in that room in the stadium?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO ALVIR
utterances.text: A total of about 300 people in the stadium, I think.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you given meals?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO ALVIR
utterances.text: Yes. We received one meal during the day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before the -- before your transfer to the stadium and before the conflict actually began, could you give this Trial Chamber an idea of how much you would have weighed.

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO ALVIR
utterances.text: 92 or 93 kilos, something like that; similar to what I weigh now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And by the time you had gotten to the stadium, how much were you weighing?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO ALVIR
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. I know that when I managed to escape I lost between 15 and 16 kilos.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. [Microphone not activated] Did you remain at the stadium all the time or were you transferred to --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you remain at the stadium all the time, or were you transferred to another area?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO ALVIR
utterances.text: They would take us to carry out work. They would take us to Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Pajic Polje, and they would take us to dig trenches from there, to Durovar Dolac [phoen].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you be able to assist the Trial Chamber as in to who -- as to who guarded you during this time in your -- in your detention at Pajic and while -- during your forced labour, digging of trenches, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO ALVIR
utterances.text: They were the units of theirs from Bugojno who were billeted in the school in Pajic Polje. I knew some men who were from Bugojno, so these were troops from Bugojno.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you able to or could you recognise who was in charge? Would you be able to assist us as to who you thought might have been in charge of the group; who supervised you at the trenches?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO ALVIR
utterances.text: Well, the man who was in command, I don't know his name. I only know about the men who took us from Pajic Polje to dig trenches every day. I know one man, Hanaz Dzelilovic was his name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know if he was a member of any battalion, any specific unit? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO ALVIR
utterances.text: I don't know what the name of this Bugojno unit was, but he was a member of that unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, there came a time when you left Pajic. Could you tell us by what means you left.

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO ALVIR
utterances.text: On the 20th of September, their commander who was there, he wanted six men for digging. That day we needed to cover up a dugout which we had dug before, and he wanted six men to go and do this work. I volunteered and asked, "Could I go," and he said, "Yes." And that day we went up there to do that work. I had decided to escape that day, and I managed to escape from one line to the other, which means from the lines of the BH army to the HVO lines, a place called Osojnica Ploca together with two other colleagues, Miroslav Marjanovic and Zivko Borislav. The three of us managed to escape and the four stayed behind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From the HVO position in Uskoplje, did you go on to any other village?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO ALVIR
utterances.text: I went to Uskoplje, and then from there to the Republic of Croatia, the town called Trogir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Whilst in Trogir, did you seek medical attention?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO ALVIR
utterances.text: Yes. I went to Livno, because that was where our hospital was. So I went to Livno for treatment. I was x-rayed immediately, and they told me I had a fracture of the fifth and sixth rib, and I continued treatment until after the new year, when I rejoined the units again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you ever able to be reunited with your immediate family members, your wife and child?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO ALVIR
utterances.text: Yes, in Trogir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Alvir, could you tell this Trial Chamber to date how you feel physically.

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO ALVIR
utterances.text: I feel quite well, only I have problems when it gets very cold. My back aches, my arms and legs. I have some problems with my back, probably due to the beatings that I received.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And could you tell us how this whole experience has affected you mentally, if it has. Could you tell us.

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO ALVIR
utterances.text: Any reminder of these things is a strain, a stress. But what can we do? That's how it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And finally, could you tell the Trial Chamber where you reside presently.

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO ALVIR
utterances.text: In Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Alvir.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, this concludes the examination-in-chief of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Ms. Benjamin. It is now 5.35. We need to have our technical break. We will resume work at 6.00 sharp. And I believe that the cross-examination will begin then. So we'll resume at 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The hearing is resumed. Without further ado, not to take away the time of the Defence, I give them the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Cross-examined by Ms. Residovic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good evening, Mr. Zrinko. My name is Edina Residovic, and I am Defence counsel for General Hadzihasanovic. I would like to ask you to answer a few questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before that, Mr. President, as the witness was a military policeman in the HVO and is a native of Bugojno, I will ask him just a few questions of a general nature regarding the military and general background that preceded these events.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So understand I will ask you some general questions first. Mr. Zrinko, you said that you were born and that you lived your whole life in Bugojno; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO ALVIR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Bugojno is in the upper course of the Vrbas River; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO ALVIR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Going from Bugojno towards Sarajevo and Zenica, one normally passes through Donji Vakuf, Komar, the Lasva Travnik, the Lasva crossroads, and then for Zenica and Sarajevo; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO ALVIR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: However, under conditions of war, due to the temporarily occupied territory of Donji Vakuf and Komar, a side road was used through Ravno Rostovo and Novi Travnik. The roads towards Herzegovina or the routes went via Gornji Vakuf, Prozor, and Jablanica, and then again because of the occupation of a part of the territory south of Jablanica, mountain roads were used to go to Mostar.

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO ALVIR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Being an inhabitant of Bugojno and a military policeman, you were aware that in 1992 and 1993 the question of the openness of traffic routes was of vital importance for Central Bosnia, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO ALVIR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Many misunderstandings and conflicts were linked to the blocking of roads; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO ALVIR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Since you probably travelled frequently between Bugojno and Gornji Vakuf, a territory which is about 18 kilometres long, I would like to ask you to have a look at a map and to recognise it first and then to point to a few locations which are of interest from the standpoint of this conversation of ours.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So could this map be shown to the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Zrinko, do you recognise this area and this road?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO ALVIR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is this the route leading from Bugojno towards Gornji Vakuf?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO ALVIR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, in view of the fact that the witness has recognised the map, I would like to tender it into evidence as a Defence exhibit. But before that, I would like to ask the witness to make some markings on this map. Would you please put the map on the overhead projector so that everyone can see it on their screens.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And using a pen, will you please write where the town of Bugojno is marked a number "1."

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO ALVIR
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For the transcript, is it correct that number 1 marks the town -- the position of the town of Bugojno? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO ALVIR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you please put a number "2" where Gornji Vakuf is situated.

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO ALVIR
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And a number "3" for the location you mentioned in your testimony, and that is Pajic Polje.

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO ALVIR
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So for the transcript, number 2 is placed next to Gornji Vakuf and number 3, the location of Pajic Polje. Is it true, Mr. Zrinko, that as one leaves Bugojno in the direction of Gornji Vakuf there is a locality called Vrbanja? If you can see that place, would you put a number "4" next to it.

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO ALVIR
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true that number 4 now stands for the location of Vrbanja?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO ALVIR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Zrinko, is it correct that the HVO headquarters in Bugojno were in Tito's villa, on a hill called Gorica?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO ALVIR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you find this hill called Gorica and mark it, please.

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO ALVIR
utterances.text: With a number "5"?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, a number "5," please.

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO ALVIR
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct that number 5 is the position of Tito's villa in which in 1993 the HVO brigade Eugen Kvaternik headquarters was situated?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO ALVIR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since the witness has marked the locations of interest to me, could the witness sign and date this map. And I would ask the Trial Chamber to admit this document into evidence as a Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please put your name on the map and today's date, the 10th of February, 2004.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Witness complies]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us show the document to the Prosecution, please; to Defence counsel to check; to the accused. Mr. Registrar, will you give us an exhibit number for this document.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the exhibit number will be D28.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So D28. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Sorry, DH28.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] DH28.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true, Mr. Alvir, that the locations that you have marked, Gorica and Vrbanja, belonged to Bugojno municipality?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO ALVIR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true that Pajic Polje belonged to the municipality of Gornji Vakuf?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO ALVIR
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now let us move on to some of the questions that you responded to prior to the break. You said that on the 20th of May you joined the HVO military police; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO ALVIR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At that time, there was a state of war in Bosnia and Herzegovina by then because of the attack of the JNA and the Serb army, so the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina proclaimed a mobilisation.

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO ALVIR
utterances.text: I think so, but I am not sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: HVO units that were formed did not place themselves under the control of the TO staff of Bosnia-Herzegovina but their superior command was the Supreme Command in Grude.

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO ALVIR
utterances.text: HVO units were formed prior to units of what you call the Armija, at least in Bugojno.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That may be correct, but my question is: Was your superior command first in Tomislavgrad and then in Grude?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO ALVIR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true that on the 7th of May Mate Boban took a decision to appoint the HVO Bugojno and that shortly after that, on the 20th of May, you joined the HVO of Bugojno?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO ALVIR
utterances.text: I have no idea about the dates. I don't know those things. I didn't keep any records, and this simply didn't interest me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In answer to a question from my learned friend, you said that the military police was based in the Kalin Hotel in the centre of Bugojno; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO ALVIR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were actually the brigade police, that is, of the 104th Brigade, called Eugen Kvaternik.

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO ALVIR
utterances.text: No, we were not the brigade police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were independent military police?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO ALVIR
utterances.text: We were an independent military police unit which had its headquarters in Livno. We were known as the 2nd Battalion, and we did not belong to the Eugen Kvaternik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. However, the brigade that was formed in 1992, the HVO brigade, was the 104th Eugen Kvaternik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO ALVIR
utterances.text: I'm not sure of the number it bore.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know the name?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO ALVIR
utterances.text: Yes, Eugen Kvaternik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In February 1993, another battalion was formed, the Home Guards Battalion, which had a territorial deployment; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO ALVIR
utterances.text: There were three battalions, the 1st, 2nd, and 3rd Battalions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And they constituted the Home Guards Regiment.

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO ALVIR
utterances.text: Yes, that was the composition of that brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the headquarters of the Eugen Kvaternik Brigade were in Tito's villa, on the Gorica hill, just above the town of Bugojno; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO ALVIR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true, Mr. Alvir, that the HVO and the brigade members, the military police in both 1992 and 1993 were better equipped, had better uniforms than members of the Armija and the brigade in Bugojno that was in the process of being formed?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO ALVIR
utterances.text: Yes, they were better equipped.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Members of the army were poorly dressed. They often wore a mixture of civilian and military clothing; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO ALVIR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true that due to wartime conditions many people who had the possibility of getting hold of a uniform wore such a uniform, regardless of whether they belonged to any unit or not? It was the fashion.

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO ALVIR
utterances.text: I don't know that. I don't know what kind of fashion people resorted to. If they were in uniform, they were soldiers. At least, that was what they looked like. What do I know?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In those days in Bugojno there were many refugees arriving, especially Bosniaks from Donji Vakuf, Prozor, Kupres, Vitez, and other locations; is that right? Jajce as well?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO ALVIR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Already at the beginning of 1993 it can be said that there were more refugees than local inhabitants.

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO ALVIR
utterances.text: I don't know whether there were more, but there were a lot of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Alvir, is it true that the events and overt conflicts between the army and the HVO in the area of Gornji Vakuf, then in the areas of Vitez, Travnik had a major impact on tension and the worsening of relationships in Bugojno itself?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO ALVIR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The particularly difficult situation, in spite of the efforts made, begins sometime in May 1993; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO ALVIR
utterances.text: I think it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that what happened first was the capture and killing of three members of the army and then in reprisal the capture of 20 members of the HVO, due to which special measures were taken to calm the situation down and to have all the captives released? Were you aware of this as a military policeman?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO ALVIR
utterances.text: You have to explain more specifically where this happened and what events you are referring to. Where were these people captured, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: First of all, on the 9th of May in this area towards Pavic Polje, five members of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina were captured, and then in the night between the 9th and 10th of May another group of members of the army were captured. And that same night the army captured 20 members of the HVO. This was a major excess that occurred due to which --

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO ALVIR
utterances.text: Where did the army capture these people?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It was an excess, a major incident. Do you remember this? Because there were people taken captive on both sides, and there were efforts to resolve the conflict by peaceful means.

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO ALVIR
utterances.text: There were such instances, but I don't know specifically what you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In order to assist you, on the 9th of May 38 members of the army were captured at the checkpoint in Humac.

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO ALVIR
utterances.text: It wasn't on Humac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. A while ago you pointed out to the village of Vrbanja on the map. Is it true to say that about 600 inhabitants lived in that village before the war?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO ALVIR
utterances.text: It's possible. I don't know the number, but the village is not a big one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know anything about the fact that on the 17th of July there were two incidents, first of all at the crossroads to the Kandija village the HVO established a checkpoint, and on that same day 500 metres in the direction of Bugojno the army established its own checkpoint at which Miroslav Talenta was killed in a fight with those manning the army checkpoint? Are you aware of this incident?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO ALVIR
utterances.text: Yes, I'm very well aware of it, but the checkpoint in Vrbanja existed from the very beginning of the war and it was there all the time. So from the very beginning of the conflict with the Serbian forces, that checkpoint was in existence and it was there all the time. And the murder of Miroslav Talenta and the wounding of Drazen Milicevic and I think at the time someone called Vucak was killed - I think his first name was Miroslav - at the time it wasn't a checkpoint but the young men were returning from the swimming pool. They were in their swimming trunks. They were in their car and they fired at their car while they were driving. There wasn't a checkpoint of any kind, but they opened fire on their vehicle. They then went off the road.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You heard about that event after it had happened.

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO ALVIR
utterances.text: Yes, but on the same day, because Drazen Milicevic was wounded. He escaped from the vehicle. He tried to escape through Vrbas, over the Vrbas. A soldier caught up with him and fired at him in the water and wounded him in the arm. He went to the Hotel Kalin, which is where the military clinic was. He told us about the entire event and he said that Miroslav Talenta had been hit in the car and that he had been killed; whereas they killed Mijo Vucak in front of the house in which they would detain them, in front of the house in which they detained HVO members. They killed him in front of the door to that house.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President, but I believe that even though cross-examination should be as wide and could be as wide, I think that this bears nothing with respect to the examination-in-chief, absolutely nothing. And further, my friend continues to put five and six questions to the witness at one time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The Defence has taken note of the Prosecution's comment. I would just like to point out that we were told by the witness that he resided in Hotel Kalin. He saw the person who had escaped from the vehicle arrive in the hotel, and this person had been wounded. The name of the person is Drazen Milicevic. So to the extent that he was --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Milicevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Milicevic. He can say -- he can tell us what he saw in the hotel. He can tell us about what he witnessed. So please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Since the Prosecution has pointed out that we ought to shorten this question, I'm just going to ask the witness whether it's correct to say that what you have just told us about is something that you heard about from that wounded man.

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO ALVIR
utterances.text: Yes. And later I saw Mijo Vucak, who was dead, and Talenta was in the military hospital. I saw their dead bodies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would it be correct to say that because of that incident the Herceg-Bosna MUP and the Bosnia-Herzegovina MUP immediately formed a mixed patrol that consisted of eight members - there were four Bosniaks and four Croats in the patrol - in order to go to the site and carry out an on-site investigation?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO ALVIR
utterances.text: Yes, I think that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would it be correct to say that at the on-site investigation some HVO members attacked the BH MUP representatives and killed three of them and in fact this is what caused the conflict to break out in the town? That was the last drop in the cup.

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO ALVIR
utterances.text: Yes, I think so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll now return to a few questions that were put to you by my colleague. You said that in fact on the 24th of July you surrendered to members of the army; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO ALVIR
utterances.text: I think so. In fact, I don't know the exact date, but I do think it was the 24th of July.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: However, the conflict had not yet ceased. At the time, the fighting continued, because the HVO headquarters in Gorica continued to resist and the conflict only ended a few days after your capture. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO ALVIR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Part of the brigade -- part of the Eugen Kvaternik Brigade, managed to withdraw from the town and several thousand Croats from Bugojno withdrew with the brigade; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO ALVIR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that you were detained in the furniture shop until the 5th of August, 1993. You also stated that the soldiers who would take you out at night and maltreat you asked you to give them your good uniforms and to put on their old uniforms.

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO ALVIR
utterances.text: Yes, that happened on the very first day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would it be correct to say that some of you HVO members destroyed your uniforms on purpose? You did this deliberately to prevent them from members of the BH army getting them.

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO ALVIR
utterances.text: Well, it wasn't to prevent them from getting them, but we didn't want them to take them off us and give us dirty clothes. But it wasn't to prevent them from getting hold of our uniforms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. But you said they were members of the army.

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO ALVIR
utterances.text: Yes. But it's not what you think. I didn't want to receive their dirty clothes in exchange for my clean ones.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, you are a witness and you should try to provide appropriate answers to my questions and tell us what the reason was for destroying your uniforms. From the very first day that you spent in the furniture shop you were able to receive food from nuns and priests; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO ALVIR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just wanted to interrupt the Defence to point out that he answered your question. He said that he didn't want to give his uniform to others because the uniforms that the others had were dirty. So he's answered your question. You are telling him that he hasn't answered your question, but in fact he has. That was just a minor detail. But please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, perhaps there was a slight error in the translation. I can't see that now. But I think that the witness has answered my questions, and I accepted the answers he provided. But thank you for drawing my attention to this fact.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After being provided with treatment in the hospital, you said that you were transferred in the second half of August to the stadium that belonged to the Iskra Football Club; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO ALVIR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also said that you received food once a day. I would like to know whether you were given soup, bread, and a tin of food.

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO ALVIR
utterances.text: Well, there was some cooked food, a soup or something similar, lentils or something like that. That's what they called them. I don't know what it is. But that's what we were given.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In addition, while you were at the stadium, you were able to receive food from civilians, acquaintances, relatives, and from Caritas; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO ALVIR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At that time, you were able to go home with an escort or to go to see friends in order to wash yourselves, et cetera; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO ALVIR
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In response to a question from the Prosecution, you said that on the 10th of September you were taken to Pajic Polje, and you escaped from there ten days later. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO ALVIR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would it be correct to say - you've already answered this question, in fact; you said that Pajic Polje was in the municipality of Gornji Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO ALVIR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You didn't know who was directly in charge of the work you were involved in; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO ALVIR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In fact, you perhaps know that the territory of the municipality of Gornji Vakuf, as of June, belonged to the 6th Corps.

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO ALVIR
utterances.text: I don't know what the name of the corps were, but I know that they were soldiers from Bugojno. In Pajic Polje and in Dolac, which is where I had fled from to the line -- at the line, there were soldiers from Bugojno. So it was a Bugojno unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. But while you were in Pajic Polje, you don't know who their superior command was. You don't know that.

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO ALVIR
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you and Miroslav Marjanovic and Borislav Zivko managed to escape, you were immediately interviewed by the security service, the SIS; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO ALVIR
utterances.text: Yes. We spoke to some people there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In addition, with regard to your experience while in detention, you gave a statement to the police station in Bugojno in November 1994; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO ALVIR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You recognised some of the men who had beaten you on the 5th of August, Vrban Edin. I don't know what the name of the other one was. Durakovic Sacir. Criminal proceedings were instituted, and you were heard as a witness in that case. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO ALVIR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Alvir. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO ALVIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll now give the floor to the other Defence team, if they have any questions to ask the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Since this testimony did you want concern the counts in the indictment with which Mr. Kubura has been charged, we have no questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I'll turn to Mrs. Benjamin to ask if she has any further questions in the light of the questions put to the witness in the course of the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, the Prosecution just has one question for this witness. Re-examined by Ms. Henry-Benjamin:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In line 15, 16, 17 -- in line 17, my learned friend asked you if criminal proceedings were instituted and if you were a witness in that such case. Could you tell the Trial Chamber when these criminal proceedings were instituted and by whom.

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO ALVIR
utterances.text: I first gave a statement at the high court in Vitez, and then I also gave a statement in Travnik in those proceedings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you give us an idea of date, time, when.

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO ALVIR
utterances.text: I don't know the exact dates.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And not -- not particularly a date, but a period of time. What year? Can you assist us?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO ALVIR
utterances.text: It was last year, I think. Three or four months ago. About four months ago. I think that's when I gave my last statement in Travnik, but I don't know the exact date.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Alvir.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, this is it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to thank the Prosecution. Witness, we have now concluded your testimony. The Prosecution has asked you all the questions that they thought were relevant, and the Defence has also asked you some questions. The Judges did not feel it was necessary to ask you any questions in order to clarify certain issues. Therefore, we have concluded your testimony. The Trial Chamber wishes you a good trip home, since you have come from quite far. And I will now ask the usher to escort you out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before we adjourn, could the Prosecution inform us of its schedule for tomorrow and tell us about the identity of the witnesses who will be heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, for that purpose can we please go into private session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We are going to go into private session, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 11th day of February, 2004, at 2.15 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 6.49 p.m.,
